concepts.name: Electric charge
concepts.statement: A physical quantity not previously introduced, electric charge, explains the effects of static electricity. There are only two types of charge, one called positive and the other called negative. We know there are two because rubbing certain materials together in controlled ways always produces one type on one material and the opposite type on the other. Glass rubbed with silk becomes positive and the silk negative, and the names are a convention that goes back to Franklin.

concepts.name: Like charges repel
concepts.statement: Two glass rods rubbed with silk repel one another, since each carries positive charge, and two silk cloths so rubbed repel too, while the rod and the silk attract because their charges are opposite. The force between charges decreases with distance. These two facts explain static cling, the balloon on the wall and the hair that stands on end. Coulomb’s law will later say exactly how the force depends on the charges and their separation.

concepts.name: Charges of the electron and proton
concepts.statement: Normal matter is made of atoms, and atoms contain positive and negative charges, usually in equal amounts. In the planetary model, negative electrons orbit a much heavier positive nucleus whose charge is due to its protons; the neutron carries no charge. Nearly all charge in nature is due to electrons and protons, whose charges are identical in magnitude but opposite in sign, and the other charged particles seen in cosmic rays and accelerators survive only a short time.

concepts.name: Elementary charge
concepts.statement: All charged objects in nature are integral multiples of one basic quantity of charge, the magnitude of the charge on a single electron or proton, $|q_\text{e}| = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}$ C. The symbol $q$ stands for charge, and the subscript e marks the charge of a single electron or proton. No directly observed charge is smaller than this. The quarks inside a proton carry $-\tfrac13$ and $+\tfrac23$ of it, but no one has ever seen a quark alone.

concepts.name: Counting the charges in a charge
concepts.statement: The SI unit of charge is the coulomb, and the number of protons needed to make 1.00 C is $6.25 \times 10^{18}$, one coulomb divided by the charge on one proton. The same number of electrons carries $-1.00$ C. To turn any charge into a count of electrons, divide by $|q_\text{e}|$. To turn a count of electrons moved through a wire or removed from a neutral object back into coulombs, multiply.

concepts.name: Rubbing separates existing charge
concepts.statement: Rubbing materials together separates charges in atoms and molecules. Some atoms and molecules have a greater affinity for electrons than others and become negatively charged by close contact, leaving the other material positively charged. Batteries separate charge by chemical interactions instead. Separating charges in this way creates and destroys none; it only moves existing charges about. For macroscopic objects, negatively charged means an excess of electrons and positively charged a depletion of them.

concepts.name: Conservation of charge
concepts.statement: Total charge is constant in any process. Rubbing only moves existing charge about. Even in a particle accelerator, where energy becomes mass in the amount $\Delta m = E/c^2$, every charged particle appears together with another of opposite charge, so the total charge created is zero. When a particle and its antimatter counterpart annihilate, the total charge is zero before and after. No experiment has ever found the law violated. Charge joins energy, momentum and angular momentum on the short list of quantities that nature always conserves.

concepts.name: Static electricity
concepts.statement: Static electricity is a buildup of electric charge on the surface of an object. It is what makes a comb rubbed through dry hair attract bits of paper and a sock cling to a sweater from the dryer.

concepts.name: Electromagnetic force
concepts.statement: The electromagnetic force is one of the four basic forces of nature. It consists of the static electric forces between charges, the magnetic forces between moving charges and magnets, and the electromagnetic waves that carry them through space.

concepts.name: Electron
concepts.statement: The electron is a particle orbiting the nucleus of an atom and carrying the smallest unit of negative charge.

concepts.name: Proton
concepts.statement: The proton is a particle in the nucleus of an atom carrying a positive charge equal in magnitude to the charge of the electron, and it is far more massive.

concepts.name: Conductor
concepts.statement: Some substances, such as metals and salty water, allow charges to move through them with relative ease. Some of the electrons in metals are not bound to individual atoms, and these free electrons can move through the material much as air moves through loose sand; salty water and similar materials contain free ions instead, an ion being an atom or molecule with a nonzero total charge. Any substance that has free electrons or free ions and allows charge to move relatively freely through it is a conductor.

concepts.name: Insulator
concepts.statement: Other substances, such as glass, do not allow charges to move through them; these are insulators. Electrons and ions in insulators are bound in the structure and cannot move easily, as much as $10^{23}$ times more slowly than in conductors. Pure water and dry table salt are insulators, whereas molten salt and salty water are conductors, and the rubber and plastic round a wire keep its charge from escaping outward.

concepts.name: Charging by contact
concepts.statement: Touching an object with a charged object charges it with the same sign. When a positively charged glass rod touches the ball of an electroscope, the rod attracts electrons to the top of the electroscope and some pass to the rod. The electroscope keeps a net positive charge, whose repulsion separates the light gold leaves, and the rod loses some of its excess charge in the transfer. Because the rod is an insulator, it must actually touch the electroscope to transfer charge.

concepts.name: Polarization
concepts.statement: Polarization is the separation of charges in an object that remains neutral. When a charged rod comes near a neutral conductor, it attracts charge of the opposite sign to the near side and leaves like charge on the far side. In an insulator the distribution of charge in each atom or molecule shifts slightly. Some molecules, like water, are polar, with a natural separation of charge although they are neutral overall.

concepts.name: Grounding
concepts.statement: A conductor is grounded when a conducting wire runs from it to the ground. Since the earth is large and most ground is a good conductor, it can supply or accept excess charge easily. A grounded conductor loses any excess charge to the earth, or draws from it whatever a nearby charge attracts. Breaking the ground connection before you remove a nearby charged object leaves the conductor with a net charge.

concepts.name: Charging by induction
concepts.statement: You can charge an object without transferring excess charge to it directly. A charged rod brought near two touching neutral spheres attracts opposite charge to the near sphere and leaves the other with like charge. Separate the spheres before you pull the rod away, and each keeps a net charge. You can charge a single sphere the same way by grounding it while the rod is near, then breaking the ground connection. The object charged by induction receives the opposite charge to the rod, and the rod loses none of its excess charge, so you can repeat the process.

concepts.name: Attraction of neutral objects
concepts.statement: Any charged object, positive or negative, attracts neutral objects. When a charged rod comes near a neutral substance, it attracts opposite charge nearer and repels like charge. The electrostatic force decreases with distance, so the repulsion of the like charges, which are farther away, is weaker than the attraction of the unlike charges, which are nearer. The net force is an attraction. That is why polished amber picks up straw, a comb picks up paper, and a charged rod bends a stream of water.

concepts.name: Free charge
concepts.statement: A free charge is an electric charge that can move about separately from its atom or molecule. In metals some electrons are not bound to individual atoms, and these free electrons carry charge through the material.

concepts.name: Free electron
concepts.statement: A free electron is an electron that is free to move away from its atomic orbit. Metals are good conductors because some of their electrons are free.

concepts.name: Electrostatic repulsion
concepts.statement: Electrostatic repulsion is the phenomenon of two objects with like charges repelling each other.

concepts.name: Coulomb’s law
concepts.statement: The main features of the electrostatic force are two types of charge, like charges repelling and unlike attracting, and the decrease of the force with distance. In the late eighteenth century Charles Coulomb turned them into the formula named for him. Coulomb’s law gives the magnitude of the force between two point charges separated by a distance $r$. It is proportional to the product of the charges and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them. Modern experiments have verified the inverse square to one part in $10^{16}$ and found no exception, even within the atom.

concepts.name: Coulomb’s constant
concepts.statement: In SI units the constant in Coulomb’s law is $k = 8.988 \times 10^{9}\ \text{N}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{C}^2$, usually rounded to $8.99 \times 10^{9}$. Its size is what makes a coulomb such a large amount of charge: two charges of 1 C each, held 1 m apart, would push on one another with a force of nearly $10^{10}$ N, which is why the charges of everyday static electricity are nanocoulombs and microcoulombs.

concepts.name: Direction of the Coulomb force
concepts.statement: The electrostatic force is a vector quantity expressed in newtons, and it is understood to be along the line joining the two charges, repulsive for like charges and attractive for unlike. Newton’s third law applies as usual: the force on $q_1$ is equal in magnitude and opposite in direction to the force $q_1$ exerts on $q_2$, whatever the sizes of the two charges.

concepts.name: Scaling the Coulomb force
concepts.statement: Because the force is proportional to each charge and inversely proportional to the square of the separation, a change in any one of them changes the force by a factor that can be read off without evaluating the constant. Halving the distance multiplies the force by four, tripling it divides by nine, doubling one charge doubles the force, and a change of the force by a factor of 10 needs a change of the distance by $\sqrt{10} \approx 3.2$ either way.

concepts.name: Coulomb force versus gravity
concepts.statement: For an electron and a proton the ratio of the electrostatic force to the gravitational force is $2.27 \times 10^{39}$, at any separation, since both fall off as the inverse square and the distance cancels in the ratio. Gravity is therefore completely negligible where individual charged particles interact. On a large scale the reverse is true: most objects are nearly electrically neutral, so the attractive and repulsive Coulomb forces nearly cancel, while gravity, which is always attractive, adds up and dominates between large objects.

forms.condition: an electron and a proton, at any separation

concepts.name: Electrostatic force
concepts.statement: The electrostatic force, also called the Coulomb force, is the attraction or repulsion between two charged bodies, with both a magnitude and a direction. Coulomb's law gives it for point charges.

concepts.name: Coulomb force field
concepts.statement: A field maps the force that surrounds any object and acts on another object at a distance without apparent physical connection, as the gravitational field of the earth maps the force a mass would feel at any point. The Coulomb force field surrounding a charge $Q$ extends throughout space, and Coulomb’s law gives its magnitude as $F = k|qQ|/r^2$ on a test charge $q$. Both its magnitude and its direction depend on the test charge as well as on $Q$, so it is not unique at any point in space.

concepts.name: Point charge and test charge
concepts.statement: The charge that creates a field is a point charge, written $Q$, and the charge set down in the field to feel it is a test charge, written $q$. The test charge is taken to be positive, so that the field has the direction of the force on it, and so small that it does not alter the charge distribution creating the field.

concepts.name: Electric field
concepts.statement: To have a field that depends only on the charge creating it, the electric field is defined as the ratio of the Coulomb force to the positive test charge it acts on. So defined, it represents only the charge creating it and is unique at every point in space, its direction is the direction of the force on a positive test charge, and its units are newtons per coulomb. It is a vector, and fields due to several charges add like vectors.

concepts.name: Force on a charge in a field
concepts.statement: If the electric field is known, the electrostatic force on any charge $q$ is obtained by multiplying the charge by the field. The force on a positive charge is in the direction of the field, and the force on a negative charge is opposite to it, which is what a negative sign on $q$ says.

concepts.name: Field of a point charge
concepts.statement: Applying the definition of the field to Coulomb’s force on a test charge, the test charge cancels and the magnitude of the electric field of a point charge is $E = k|Q|/r^2$. The field depends only on the charge $Q$ and the distance $r$ from it, and is completely independent of the test charge; it points away from a positive $Q$ and toward a negative one.

concepts.name: Direction of the electric field
concepts.statement: Because the field is defined for a positive test charge, it points away from a positive charge and toward a negative charge, and the force on a charge placed in it is along the field for a positive charge and against it for a negative one. A field found to be positive in a calculation is a field pointing away from the charge that creates it.

concepts.name: Point charge
concepts.statement: A point charge, designated $Q$, is a charged particle that generates an electric field.

concepts.name: Electric field lines
concepts.statement: Since the electric field has both magnitude and direction, it is a vector, and you can draw it at any point as an arrow whose length is its magnitude. The standard picture replaces the arrows with continuous field lines that have the same direction at any point as the field, and the closeness of the lines shows the strength of the field. Field lines are a map of infinitesimal force vectors, a pictorial tool and not a physical entity. Gravitational, magnetic and other fields use the same picture.

concepts.name: Properties of electric field lines
concepts.statement: For any charge distribution, field lines begin on positive charges and end on negative charges, or at infinity for an isolated charge. The number of lines leaving a positive charge or entering a negative one is proportional to the magnitude of the charge. The strength of the field is proportional to the number of lines per unit area perpendicular to them. The field of a point charge falls as $1/r^2$, and its lines spread over an area that grows as $r^2$, so they show it exactly. The direction of the field is tangent to the line at any point. Field lines can never cross, since the field is unique at every point and a crossing would give it two directions.

concepts.name: Superposition of electric fields
concepts.statement: In many situations there are multiple charges, and the total electric field they create at a point is the vector sum of the individual fields created by each charge. The field of each charge at the point is found from $E = k|Q|/r^2$ with the direction of the force on a positive test charge there, and the fields are then added with the same vector techniques used for forces and velocities.

concepts.name: Adding the fields of two charges
concepts.statement: To find the total field at a point, find the field of each charge there in magnitude and direction, pretending a positive test charge sits at the point to fix the directions, then add the vectors. When the two fields are perpendicular, as in Example 18.4, the Pythagorean theorem gives the magnitude and the inverse tangent gives the direction; otherwise components or graphical techniques are used.

concepts.name: Finding the total force from several charges
concepts.statement: The total force on a charge is the vector sum of the Coulomb forces the other charges exert on it, each along the line joining the pair and each found from Coulomb’s law. Equivalently, it is the charge multiplied by the total electric field at its position. Symmetry often settles the direction before you enter any number, and the net force is zero wherever the individual forces cancel.

concepts.name: Field of two charges
concepts.statement: The field of two point charges can be drawn by finding the total field at representative points and drawing lines consistent with them. Between two like charges the field is weaker, the lines farther apart, because the fields of the two charges oppose one another there, and at a great distance the field becomes that of a single larger charge. Between two unlike charges the field is stronger, since the two fields point the same way, and at large distances it is weak, since the two fields subtract, looking like the field of a smaller single charge.

concepts.name: Sketching electric field lines
concepts.statement: A field-line drawing is built from the five properties: lines leave positive charges and enter negative ones in numbers proportional to the charges, they never cross, their direction is the field’s and their closeness is its strength. Near a single charge the lines are radial, near two charges they bend as Figures 18.22 and 18.23 show, and far from any distribution they look like the lines of one charge equal to the total.

concepts.name: Large biological molecules are charged
concepts.statement: Classical electrostatics has an important role in molecular biology, because the large molecules so important to life, proteins and nucleic acids, are usually electrically charged. DNA carries about two fundamental charges per 0.3 nm along its length, and it is the electrostatic force that holds the molecule together and gives it its structure and strength; since the Coulomb force falls as $1/r^2$, the base pairs must be close enough, about 0.3 nm within a base and 1 nm between the strands, for the force to hold them.

concepts.name: Polar molecules and dipoles
concepts.statement: Water is a strongly polar molecule: its ten electrons tend to remain closer to the oxygen nucleus than to the hydrogen nuclei, which creates two centers of equal and opposite charge, a dipole, whose magnitude is the dipole moment. The oxygen side is slightly negative and the hydrogen ends slightly positive, and the attraction of opposite charges between molecules follows. A molecule with a natural separation of charge is more strongly affected by other charges than one with a uniform distribution.

concepts.name: Electrostatic screening
concepts.statement: Many molecules in living things are charged, yet electrostatic forces play a smaller role in biology than you might expect, because screening dilutes them. The two centers of charge in a water molecule, and the Na⁺, K⁺ and Cl⁻ ions inside and outside cells, end some of the field lines coming from a free charge and weaken the Coulomb interaction. Screening makes the Coulomb force a short-range force rather than a long-range one. Microtubules within a cell may still extend electric fields over larger distances.

concepts.name: Dipole
concepts.statement: A dipole is a pair of separated centers of equal and opposite charge, such as a molecule whose charge is not symmetrically distributed, so that one side is more positive and the other more negative.

concepts.name: Electrostatic equilibrium
concepts.statement: Conductors contain free charges that move easily. When you place excess charge on a conductor or put it in a static electric field, the charges quickly reach a steady state called electrostatic equilibrium. The free charges move until no force remains to move them, and every property of a conductor in equilibrium follows from that condition. In metals the free charges are electrons, but a positive charge moving one way is equivalent to a negative charge moving the other.

concepts.name: Field at the surface of a conductor
concepts.statement: There can be no component of the field parallel to the surface of a conductor in electrostatic equilibrium, since if there were it would exert a force $F_\parallel = qE_\parallel$ on the free charges and produce further movement of charge. The free charges move until the field is perpendicular to the surface, so just outside a conductor the field lines are perpendicular to it, ending or beginning on charges on the surface.

concepts.name: Field inside a conductor
concepts.statement: An electric field polarizes a conductor placed in it. Its free charges move until the field lines end on excess negative charge on one part of the surface and begin again on excess positive charge on the opposite side. No field remains inside, since free charges would keep moving in response to any field until they cancelled it. The field outside becomes stronger near the conductor and disappears entirely within it.

concepts.name: Excess charge on a conductor’s surface
concepts.statement: Excess charges on a spherical conductor repel one another and move until they spread evenly over its surface, where they stay once the field inside is zero. Any excess charge resides entirely on the surface or surfaces of a conductor. Outside a charged sphere the field is exactly that of a point charge at its center equal to the excess charge.

concepts.name: Field between parallel plates
concepts.statement: Two metal plates with equal and opposite excess charges create a very uniform electric field. The properties of conductors in equilibrium spread the charges uniformly except near the edges. The field lines are therefore uniformly spaced, so the field is uniform in strength, and perpendicular to the flat surfaces, so it is uniform in direction. The edge effects matter less when the plates are close together. Such a field gives charges a uniform acceleration, as in the electron gun of an old cathode-ray tube.

concepts.name: Earth’s electric field
concepts.statement: A near-uniform electric field of about 150 N/C, directed downward, surrounds Earth, maintained in fair weather between the positive ionosphere, a layer of charged particles about 100 km up, and the largely negative Earth, both of which are conductors. In storm conditions clouds form and local fields can be larger and reversed; if the field exceeds about $3 \times 10^{6}$ N/C the insulating air breaks down and becomes conducting, and the discharge is lightning or corona.

concepts.name: Charge concentration at points
concepts.statement: On a nonuniform conductor the excess charges become concentrated at the sharpest points. The forces between identical pairs of charges at either end of the conductor are the same, but only the component parallel to the surface moves charge apart. That component is greatest on the flattest surface and smallest at the most pointed end, so the charges end up closer together at the point. The field, which must meet the surface at right angles, is strongest there. An external field polarizes a conductor the same way, with its most concentrated charge at its most pointed end.

concepts.name: Lightning rods and smooth conductors
concepts.statement: On a very sharply curved surface the charges are so concentrated that the field can pull them off the surface. Lightning rods work best when they are most pointed, because the point continually bleeds away the charge a storm cloud induces on a building and so prevents the more dramatic strike. To prevent the transfer of charge instead, as on a high-voltage transmission line or the terminal of a Van de Graaff generator, make the conductor very smooth, with as large a radius of curvature as possible.

concepts.name: Faraday cage
concepts.statement: A Faraday cage is a metal shield that encloses a volume: all electrical charges reside on its outside surface and there is no electric field inside, so it keeps stray fields in the environment from interfering with sensitive measurements such as the signals inside a nerve cell. A car’s metal body is a Faraday cage, which is why it is best to stay inside it during an electrical storm or if a live wire has fallen on it, provided you remain totally inside.

concepts.name: Ionosphere
concepts.statement: The ionosphere is a layer of charged particles about 100 km above the surface of Earth. It is positive, and with the largely negative Earth it maintains the fair-weather electric field.

concepts.name: Van de Graaff generator
concepts.statement: A Van de Graaff generator uses both smooth and pointed surfaces, and conductors and insulators, to build large static charges and hence large voltages. A pointed conductor sprays charge onto a moving insulating belt near the bottom. A second pointed conductor inside the large sphere picks it off at the top, and the charge moves to the sphere’s outside surface. A very large excess charge builds up before the field polarizes and ionizes the surrounding material and lets it escape. Van de Graaff built the first in 1931 for nuclear physics research, and voltages of 15 million volts are practical.

concepts.name: Xerography and the laser printer
concepts.statement: Most copy machines use xerography, a dry copying process based on electrostatics. Points spray positive charge onto a selenium-coated aluminum drum. Selenium is a photoconductor, an insulator in the dark and a conductor in the light, so where the image is light the charge leaks away to the grounded drum, and where it is dark the positive charge remains. The charged regions attract negatively charged toner. A paper given a greater positive charge pulls the toner off the drum, and heated rollers melt it into the fibers. A laser printer makes the image on the drum with a scanned laser beam and is otherwise the same process.

concepts.name: Ink jet printer
concepts.statement: An ink jet printer makes a fine spray of tiny ink droplets and gives them an electrostatic charge. Pairs of charged plates then direct them with great precision to form letters and images on paper, and a black jet and three colored jets produce color. Electrostatic painting charges paint the same way. Mutual repulsion of like charges makes the paint fly from its source, and surface tension forms drops. The unlike charge of the surface draws them in, perpendicular to a conductor and with extra paint on corners and points.

concepts.name: Electrostatic precipitators and air cleaning
concepts.statement: An electrostatic air cleaner places excess charge, usually positive, on the smoke, dust, pollen and other particles in the air and then passes the air through an oppositely charged grid that attracts and retains them. Large precipitators remove over 99% of the particles from the stack gas of coal- and oil-fired plants, and home units remove polluting particles, irritants and allergens.

concepts.name: Solving electrostatics problems
concepts.statement: First examine the situation to see whether static electricity plays a part. Identify the system with the number, locations and types of charges. List the unknowns and decide whether you need the Coulomb force directly; if so, a free-body diagram drawn with field lines helps. List the knowns, keeping the Coulomb force $F$ distinct from the electric field $E$. Solve the appropriate equation or draw the field lines. Then check the answer for reasonable size, sign and units. An unreasonable answer usually points to the premise that produced it, such as an excessively large separated charge.

concepts.name: Joining electrostatics to Newton’s laws
concepts.statement: The electric field exerts a force on charges, and so the problems of electrostatics reach into dynamics, kinematics, circular motion, statics and fluids. The strategy is to identify the physical principles involved and the chapters they come from, then solve each part with that part’s own strategy: weight from $w = mg$, the electric force from $F = qE$, the acceleration from Newton’s second law with the net force, and the motion that follows from the kinematics of constant acceleration.

concepts.name: Electrostatics
concepts.statement: Electrostatics is the study of electric forces that are static or slow-moving. Its ideas are put to work in machines such as the Van de Graaff generator, the copier and the electrostatic precipitator.

concepts.name: Photoconductor
concepts.statement: A photoconductor is a substance that is an insulator until it is exposed to light, when it becomes a conductor. Selenium is one.

concepts.name: Laser printer
concepts.statement: A laser printer uses a laser to create a photoconductive image on a drum, which attracts dry ink particles that are then rolled onto paper.
